## Today's Agenda

- The Facebook emotional contagion study, and the reaction to it
- Three cases that produced today's rules: Tuskegee, Milgram, and Humphreys
- The Belmont principles and institutional review
- Whether the example dataset is human subjects research
- Honest reporting, and the CITI training that is due

## Facebook Manipulated 700,000 News Feeds

[Kramer, Guillory, and Hancock, 2014]{.eyebrow}

- For one week in January 2012, Facebook manipulated users' News Feeds
- Some users saw fewer positive posts from friends, and others saw fewer negative posts
- Researchers then measured what those users posted themselves
- The manipulation worked: less positive input produced slightly more negative output
- The result was published in *PNAS* as evidence of **massive-scale emotional contagion**

## The Reaction to the Study

- Nearly 700,000 people were enrolled with **no informed consent**
- No one was told, and no one could decline

::: {.define}
**Informed consent:** a person's voluntary agreement to take part in a study, given after they are told what it involves, its risks, and that they can stop at any time without penalty. Example: a viewer reads what your interview study involves, including that they can quit, and then agrees to take part.
:::

## Two Sides of the Argument

- Facebook argued its terms of service authorized "research"
- The researchers argued the effect was tiny and the knowledge valuable
- *PNAS* appended an **editorial expression of concern**, an unusual step

## Ethics Is a Disposition, Not a Form

- It is tempting to treat ethics as a training module standing between you and the data
- Ethics shapes how you think about your relationship to the people you study
- It governs how honestly you report what you find
- The protections exist because researchers **caused real harm**, systematically
- Reasonable people still disagree about the Facebook study, and that disagreement is the point

## Tuskegee, 1932 to 1972

- The U.S. Public Health Service studied untreated syphilis in **399 Black men**
- The men were told they were receiving free treatment for "bad blood"
- Penicillin became the standard treatment in the 1940s, and the researchers **withheld it**
- 28 men died directly of syphilis, 100 died of complications, 40 wives were infected, and 19 children were born with congenital syphilis
- The study was federally funded, peer-reviewed, and unchallenged for forty years

## Milgram, 1961

- Participants were recruited by newspaper advertisement and told it was a study of memory and learning
- Each was cast as the "teacher," while a confederate played the "learner" in the next room
- They were told to deliver escalating shocks for wrong answers, up to a switch marked **450 volts**
- The shocks were not real. The belief that they were, and the distress, were real
- **26 of 40** participants in the baseline condition went all the way to the maximum
- Hesitation got a scripted prod, "the experiment requires that you continue," rather than permission to stop

## Milgram, What It Cost

- Milgram reported participants sweating, trembling, and stuttering, and one seizure violent enough to stop the session
- The deception was total until the debriefing afterward
- The findings reshaped how the field understands obedience to authority, and they are still taught in every introductory course
- Whether that knowledge justified the distress has never been settled
- That is the point: Milgram was neither careless nor malicious, and people were still harmed

## Humphreys, 1970

- Humphreys's doctoral research studied anonymous sexual encounters between men in public restrooms
- He took the role of **watchqueen**, the lookout, which let him observe without taking part and without saying he was a researcher
- He wrote down the **license plates** of the men he observed
- He traced those plates to home addresses through motor vehicle records, reached through a contact in the police
- About a year later he changed his appearance and his car, and interviewed those men in their own homes, posing as a health-survey interviewer

## Humphreys, What It Cost

- Most of the men were married and living otherwise conventional lives
- In 1970 exposure meant criminal prosecution, lost jobs, and ruined families
- He kept the data secure, and he argued the work reduced stigma by showing who these men actually were
- The book won a major award in sociology, and his own department fought over whether to take his doctorate away
- Both of those are true at once, which is why the case is still assigned

## The Common Thread

- Every one of these researchers believed the work served a greater good
- Every one produced participants who were harmed, deceived, or exploited
- **Good intentions are not sufficient protection**
- Researchers need external accountability and formal principles
- Tuskegee's exposure in 1972 produced the framework we use today

## Exercise: Was It Consent? {.discuss}

Answer each in writing:

- Facebook says the terms of service covered the study. State whether that counts as consent, and give one reason
- Say whether a tiny effect changes your answer, and why
- Name one feature that separates a company's A/B test from a psychology experiment

## Belmont: Respect for Persons

[National Commission, 1979]{.eyebrow}

::: {.define}
**Respect for persons:** treating people as able to make their own decisions, and giving extra protection to people whose ability to decide is limited. Example: the Facebook users were never asked whether they wanted to take part.
:::

- **Informed consent** is how a study puts that respect into practice
- **Vulnerable populations** get extra protection: children, prisoners, and people with cognitive impairments, whose voluntary consent is compromised
- Public social media complicates this principle, and the slides on the example dataset come back to it

## Belmont: Beneficence

::: {.define}
**Beneficence:** the duty to do no harm, and to make a study's possible benefits as large, and its possible harms as small, as you can. Example: quoting chat messages without usernames, so no viewer is singled out.
:::

- Harm here means physical, psychological, social, or economic injury to participants
- The knowledge a study produces must justify the risk it creates

## Belmont: Justice

::: {.define}
**Justice:** sharing the burdens and the benefits of research fairly, so no group carries the risk while others gain the knowledge. Example: recruiting from one group only because it is easy to reach would raise a justice question.
:::

- Tuskegee violated justice directly: all the risk fell on a marginalized population, and the knowledge accrued to everyone else

## Institutional Review

::: {.define}
**Institutional Review Board (IRB):** the committee that oversees research involving people, reviewing each study before it starts to protect the people in it. Example: SIUE's IRB decides whether a study of public chat counts as human subjects research.
:::

- It reviews a study **before** data collection for risk minimization, equitable selection, consent, privacy, and confidentiality
- **The IRB makes the determination, not you.** You submit, and the board decides

## Three Levels of Review

::: {.define}
**Expedited review:** review by the IRB chair or an experienced member, rather than the whole board, for research with no more than minimal risk in categories federal rules list. Example: many surveys and interview studies with adults.
:::

::: {.define}
**Full board review:** review at a meeting with a majority of the IRB's members present, for research that is neither exempt nor eligible for expedited review. Example: a study that carries more than minimal risk to its participants.
:::

- **Exempt** status is for minimal-risk studies inside categories that federal regulation names

## The Question That Comes First

Before any of that, there is a prior question: **is this human subjects research at all?**

::: {.define}
**Human subject:** under federal rules, a living person about whom a researcher gets information by interacting with them or intervening in their lives, or gets identifiable private information. Example: a viewer you interview.
:::

- You never interact with anyone, because the messages were sent before you arrived
- The messages were **broadcast publicly**, so they are not private information
- Neither part is met, so this is **not human subjects research**, and the three review levels never come into it

## The Example Dataset Through Belmont

- The data was collected from Twitch's **public IRC interface** and **public API**
- It holds no IP addresses, no emails, no user IDs, no payment data, and no whispers
- Usernames are present but **pseudonymous**: chosen handles, not legal names
- **Respect for persons:** the case rests on public broadcast, not on consent
- **Beneficence:** the risk is minimal. **Justice:** no group bears a disproportionate burden
- You run the same walkthrough on the source you choose, and your answers may differ

## This Determination Has Been Made Twice

- **This is not hypothetical.** Michigan State University formally determined the Twitch data **not human subjects research**, and SIUE determined the Twitter data from the NSF work the same way
- **Your project is expected to land in the same place:** a content analysis of public broadcast content is not human subjects research
- **The university makes that call, never the researcher.** You file nothing for this course, because the determination already exists for this data
- If you carry work like this past the course, into a thesis or a job, requesting the determination becomes your job
- You still complete CITI, because the training is what lets you make the argument, and because the next dataset you meet may not be this clean

## Public Does Not Mean Fair Game

- Public accessibility is not automatic permission (Markham & Buchanan, 2012)
- Do not aggregate in ways that re-identify individual users
- Do not republish entire chat logs verbatim
- Do not amplify messages whose senders expected obscurity more than broadcast
- The cleanness of this dataset is a starting point, not a license

## Three Cases That Would Be Human Subjects Research

The same research question with different data gets a different determination:

- **Twitch whispers** are private messages with a reasonable expectation of privacy, so they need expedited or full review
- **A private Discord server** with the same people has closed membership and a stronger privacy expectation, so it needs expedited or full review
- **An internal moderation log** with platform flags on named users risks harm to identified individuals, so it most likely needs **full board** review

## Consent Gets Complicated

::: {.define}
**Deception:** giving participants false or incomplete information about a study's purpose or procedures. Example: Milgram told participants the study was about memory and learning.
:::

::: {.define}
**Debriefing:** telling participants, right after data collection, what the study's real purpose was and what risks it posed to them. Example: Milgram's participants learned afterward that the shocks were not real.
:::

- Deception is sometimes justified, and it is always paired with mandatory debriefing plus the option to withdraw your data

## Passive Consent and Secondary Analysis

- **Passive consent**, the terms-of-service move, is generally insufficient, and ethicists prefer **active consent**: an affirmative act
- **Secondary analysis** of someone else's data raises whether the original consent covered your use, and it is generally acceptable when the data is de-identified
- Secondary analysis is where research ethics is still actively evolving

## Honest Reporting Is an Ethical Obligation

::: {.define}
**Fabrication:** making up data or results and reporting them. **Falsification:** manipulating research materials or processes, or changing or leaving out data or results, so the research record is no longer accurate. Example: inventing coded messages, or quietly dropping the ones that weaken your result.
:::

- Both are fraud, and both end careers

## Two Quieter Distortions

::: {.define}
**Selective reporting:** running many analyses and reporting only the ones that came out the way you hoped, which distorts the literature. Example: testing ten channels and writing up only the two that showed a difference.
:::

::: {.define}
**HARKing:** Hypothesizing After the Results are Known, then writing the hypothesis up as if you had predicted it. Example: finding that emote spam peaks during raids, then presenting that as your prediction from the start.
:::

- A postdiction carries none of a prediction's weight
- Watch for "our results suggest" quietly becoming "our results demonstrate"

## CITI, and What It Is

::: {.define}
**CITI:** the Collaborative Institutional Training Initiative, an online program of research ethics training that SIUE students, faculty, and staff reach through the university. Example: the Social and Behavioral Research course you complete for this class.
:::

- You submit the completion certificate when you finish
- The modules walk the ground we just walked: the history, the principles, consent, privacy and confidentiality, assessing risk, and vulnerable populations

## Working Through CITI

- Each module ends in a quiz you have to pass
- It takes hours rather than minutes, and it saves your place, so do it in pieces
- **CITI Ethics Certification**, 25 points, is due Friday, September 25, 11:59 PM

## Where to Register

Two pages, and the order matters:

1. **[SIUE Compliance Training](https://www.siue.edu/compliance/training/)** first. This is the route in, and it tells you how to attach your account to SIUE
2. **[CITI Program](https://www.citiprogram.org/index.cfm?pageID=668)** second, to register and work through the modules

- **Register through SIUE, not as an "independent learner."** The independent route charges you money, and the certificate does not come back to the university, so it will not count
- If you have already made an account that way, say so and we will sort it out

## Why CITI Applies to You Anyway

If your project is not human subjects research, why train for human subjects research?

- Because "this is not human subjects research" is an **argument you have to be able to make**, and CITI is where you learn to make it
- Because the moment a project touches people directly, no IRB will look at you without it
- Because it travels: graduate programs and research jobs ask to see it
- Start it this week. Somebody every term starts the night before and discovers it is not a twenty-minute task
